PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 42 — Lesson 66: Abdominal, Gastrointestinal & Hepatobiliary Assessment

FNP-level goal: Evaluate abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, GI bleeding, altered bowel habits, and jaundice with a structured differential; identify peritonitis, hemorrhage, obstruction, ischemia, pregnancy-related emergencies, sepsis, and liver decompensation; and select targeted testing, imaging, referral, or emergency disposition safely.

Learning Objectives

  • Build a time- and location-based problem representation for abdominal and GI complaints.
  • Use a safe abdominal examination sequence and recognize its diagnostic limitations.
  • Differentiate high-consequence causes of abdominal pain, vomiting, GI bleeding, and jaundice from lower-risk outpatient patterns.
  • Apply pregnancy testing, urinalysis, laboratory studies, and imaging to a specific clinical question.
  • Recognize when GI symptoms may be cardiovascular, pulmonary, gynecologic, urologic, metabolic, or medication-related.
  • Create a clear follow-up and return-precautions plan when outpatient assessment is appropriate.

Part 1 — Acute Abdomen Is a Stability Problem First

Before refining the differential, assess appearance, vital signs, perfusion, hydration, mental status, pain severity, vomiting, bleeding, and the ability to stand or move. Hypotension, tachycardia with poor perfusion, syncope, altered mental status, rigid abdomen, involuntary guarding, rebound/peritoneal concern, persistent bilious or bloody vomiting, hematemesis, melena with symptoms of hypovolemia, severe distention, or pain out of proportion to examination can signal a surgical, hemorrhagic, ischemic, infectious, or pregnancy-related emergency.

Do not extend a routine outpatient evaluation to finish a complete history when instability is present. Stabilization and emergency transfer take priority. A patient may have serious intra-abdominal disease despite initially near-normal vital signs, so trajectory and repeated assessment matter.

Part 2 — Build the Abdominal Problem Representation

Clarify onset (sudden versus gradual), location, migration, character, intensity, intermittent versus constant pattern, food relation, position/movement, associated fever, vomiting, bowel/urinary changes, bleeding, jaundice, weight loss, and prior episodes. Ask what was happening at onset: meal, alcohol or drug exposure, exertion, trauma, pregnancy possibility, travel, sick contact, surgery, immobility, or medication change.

Location helps organize, but does not prove, a diagnosis. Right-upper-quadrant pain may be biliary/hepatic but can be pulmonary, renal, GI, or referred; epigastric pain can be pancreatic, biliary, ulcer-related, cardiac, aortic, or metabolic; lower abdominal pain can be GI, urinary, gynecologic, vascular, or musculoskeletal. Build the differential from pattern plus risk, not quadrant alone.

Part 3 — Pregnancy Status Changes the Differential

For a patient with reproductive potential and abdominal/pelvic pain, bleeding, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, syncope, hypotension, urinary symptoms, or amenorrhea, assess pregnancy possibility early. A positive test with pain or bleeding requires attention to ectopic pregnancy and other pregnancy complications until appropriately evaluated. Pregnancy status also changes medication and imaging choices.

Do not assume contraception, a recent menstrual period, or a young age makes pregnancy irrelevant. Use confidential, respectful history taking. If the patient is unstable, has a positive pregnancy test with pain/bleeding, peritoneal signs, shoulder pain, syncope, or hypovolemia, emergency evaluation is required rather than an outpatient imaging order.

Part 4 — Focused Abdominal Examination

Position the patient comfortably, provide privacy and draping, ask about the most painful area, and observe before touching. Inspect for distention, scars, hernia, bruising, jaundice, visible masses, respiratory movement, and the patient’s willingness to move. Auscultate before palpation, then percuss and palpate gently, beginning away from maximal pain. Assess focal versus diffuse tenderness, guarding, rigidity, mass, organ enlargement when feasible, flank tenderness, and signs of volume depletion or chronic liver disease.

Examination findings are clues, not a substitute for imaging or urgent disposition. Absence of guarding does not exclude early appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, ischemia, or obstruction. A nonperitoneal abdomen does not cancel an alarming history of GI bleeding, severe persistent pain, unexplained weight loss, or worsening vomiting.

Part 5 — Nausea and Vomiting: Hydration, Obstruction, Metabolic Risk

Assess duration, frequency, oral intake, urine output, pregnancy possibility, blood/bile/feculent material, headache/neurologic symptoms, abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea/constipation, diabetes, kidney disease, medications, cannabis or other substance use, sick contacts, and recent procedures. Determine whether vomiting is causing dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, aspiration risk, missed medications, or inability to manage chronic disease.

Bilious vomiting, hematemesis, severe distention, obstipation, severe pain, altered mental status, significant dehydration, DKA risk, sepsis concern, or inability to take fluids safely requires urgent assessment. “Gastroenteritis” should not become a default label when the timeline, pain, bleeding, pregnancy status, or physiology does not fit.

Part 6 — GI Bleeding: Treat Perfusion and Source as Separate Questions

Ask about hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis, melena, hematochezia, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, NSAIDs, liver disease, alcohol, ulcer history, weight loss, change in bowel habit, dizziness, syncope, and prior colonoscopy/endoscopy when relevant. Upper and lower sources can overlap in presentation; stool color alone does not determine severity or location.

Assess hemodynamics, orthostatic symptoms when safe, mental status, pallor, abdominal findings, and ongoing blood loss. Melena or hematemesis with tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, severe weakness, chest pain, dyspnea, or altered mentation requires emergency evaluation. A stable patient with minor rectal bleeding still needs a thoughtful anorectal, GI, medication, and cancer-risk assessment rather than automatic reassurance.

Part 7 — Jaundice and Liver-Focused Reasoning

Jaundice reflects elevated bilirubin and may be prehepatic, hepatocellular, or cholestatic/obstructive. Ask about dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, RUQ pain, fever, nausea, fatigue, alcohol, medications and supplements, acetaminophen-containing products, viral-hepatitis risk, travel, transfusion/needle/sexual exposure where relevant, prior gallstones, liver disease, and weight loss.

New jaundice with fever/RUQ pain, confusion, bleeding tendency, ascites, hypotension, rapidly worsening symptoms, severe vomiting, or concern for acute liver failure/decompensation needs urgent evaluation. Do not attribute jaundice to a supplement, alcohol, or a medication without also considering obstruction, infection, viral hepatitis, ischemia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, and other causes.

Part 8 — Choose Laboratory Tests and Imaging With a Question

Targeted tests may include pregnancy testing, urinalysis, CBC, electrolytes/renal function, liver chemistries and bilirubin, lipase when pancreatic disease is plausible, glucose/ketones when metabolic decompensation is possible, and other studies guided by the differential. A normal early laboratory result does not necessarily end an evolving process; trends and reassessment matter.

Ultrasound can answer selected biliary, pelvic, pregnancy-related, renal, and fluid questions. CT may be useful for other acute abdominal processes when indicated. Imaging in pregnancy requires deliberate coordination, but concern for a time-sensitive maternal emergency should not be ignored or delayed. Choose the modality based on the patient, suspected condition, stability, local access, and current protocol; imaging supports clinical reasoning but does not replace emergency transfer in an unstable patient.

Part 9 — Medication and Non-GI Mimics

Medication history can alter both the differential and the safety plan. NSAIDs, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, steroids, GLP-1/GIP-GLP-1 therapies, opioids, antibiotics, iron, bismuth, diabetes medicines, alcohol, and supplements may contribute to symptoms, bleeding risk, stool changes, hepatotoxicity, constipation, pancreatitis concern, or dehydration. Do not advise abrupt cessation of a high-stakes medication without understanding the indication and coordinating a plan when necessary.

Abdominal symptoms can be extra-abdominal. Inferior ischemia, heart failure, pneumonia, PE, DKA, adrenal crisis, pyelonephritis, nephrolithiasis, abdominal aortic aneurysm, and gynecologic disease can present with nausea, vomiting, or abdominal discomfort. Revisit the whole problem representation whenever a patient’s physiology or trajectory does not fit the presumed GI diagnosis.

Part 10 — Follow-Up and Diagnostic Safety

Outpatient management is appropriate only when the patient is stable, high-consequence alternatives are reasonably addressed, oral intake and medication adherence are feasible, pain and symptoms are manageable, and follow-up is reliable. Provide specific precautions: worsening/localizing pain, fever, persistent vomiting, fainting, GI bleeding, jaundice, new chest pain or dyspnea, inability to hydrate, decreased urine output, pregnancy-related symptoms, or failure to improve should trigger urgent reassessment.

Track pending tests, review abnormal results, and document who owns referral and follow-up. A return visit with new or worsening symptoms is not simply “failure of outpatient treatment”; it is new diagnostic information that requires reassessment.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Epigastric Pain Is Not Always Gastritis

A 62-year-old with diabetes and hypertension reports new epigastric pressure, nausea, diaphoresis, and dyspnea while walking. They have mild epigastric tenderness.

FNP reasoning: GI disease is possible, but exertional symptoms and cardiometabolic risk make ACS a high-consequence alternative. Mild abdominal tenderness does not exclude cardiac ischemia. Assess stability and arrange the appropriate emergency cardiovascular evaluation.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Pain, Bleeding, and Pregnancy Risk

A 29-year-old has lower abdominal pain, light vaginal bleeding, dizziness, and a positive home pregnancy test. The abdomen is mildly tender without obvious rigidity.

FNP reasoning: pregnancy plus pain/bleeding requires ectopic-pregnancy evaluation until location and stability are established. A mild examination does not make the situation safe for delayed routine imaging if symptoms or vital signs are concerning.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: “Just a Stomach Bug” That Is Worsening

A 71-year-old with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and increasing distress. The pain appears more severe than the initial abdominal findings.

FNP reasoning: consider high-consequence causes such as mesenteric ischemia alongside obstruction, perforation, pancreatitis, and others. Severe pain out of proportion, risk context, and deterioration require urgent emergency evaluation—not repeated outpatient antiemetics.

FNP Abdominal-Assessment Framework

  1. Assess stability first: perfusion, bleeding, dehydration, peritoneal signs, mental status, and trajectory.
  2. Check pregnancy possibility: early in reproductive-age abdominal/pelvic symptom assessment.
  3. Define the pattern: onset, location/migration, food/movement relation, vomiting, bowel/urinary changes, bleeding, jaundice, and exposures.
  4. Examine safely: inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate; begin away from maximal pain.
  5. Include non-GI causes: cardiac, pulmonary, vascular, metabolic, urologic, and gynecologic conditions.
  6. Test with a question: pregnancy test, UA, CBC/chemistries, liver studies, lipase, ultrasound, CT, or emergency evaluation as indicated.
  7. Safety-net and close the loop: clear precautions, reliable result tracking, and reassessment for change in trajectory.

High-Yield Summary

Acute abdominal pain: begins with stability and emergency red flags, not a presumed GI diagnosis.
Pregnancy test: can change the differential, medication/imaging safety, and urgency.
Abdominal examination: inspect → auscultate → percuss → palpate; normal findings do not rule out evolving serious disease.
GI bleeding: assess perfusion and ongoing loss; melena/hematemesis with instability needs emergency care.
Jaundice: requires a broad hepatocellular/cholestatic/hemolytic differential and urgent escalation when systemic or decompensation signs are present.
Testing: should answer a question; imaging supports but does not replace emergency disposition.
FNP standard: integrate pattern, risk, examination, pregnancy status, targeted diagnostics, follow-up ownership, and return precautions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Assessment of abdominal pain, GI bleeding, jaundice, pregnancy-related symptoms, imaging, emergency triage, treatment, referral, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
